name: v1.16.0
body:
# v1.16.0

RestermScript gets `append`, `min`, `max` and `math.sum`, and you can use `list`, `dict`, `text` and `math` without the `rts.` prefix.

A few things that quietly gave wrong results in 1.15.0 fail in this version, such as searching a string for `null` and adding two lists or dictionaries with `+`. `@use` and `@setting` at the start of a `###` block apply to that request instead of the whole file.

## New RestermScript helpers

The `validators.rts` module from the 1.15.0 notes used `rts.list.append`. In 1.16.0 it looks like this:

```rts
module validators

export fn orders(list) {
  let errs = []
  for let _, o range list {
    if o.total < 0 {
      errs = append(errs, "order " + str(o.id) + ": total " + str(o.total) + " is negative")
    }
    if len(o.items) == 0 {
      errs = append(errs, "order " + str(o.id) + ": no items")
    }
  }
  return errs
}
```

The test output is the same as before:

```text
Tests:
  [FAIL] orders are valid - orders.http:7: order 1: total -5 is negative
                            orders.http:7: order 3: no items (82.25µs)
```

- **`append(list, items...)`** returns a new list with the items added, so `append([1], 2, 3)` is `[1, 2, 3]`. A null list counts as empty, and a list passed as an item stays one item: `append([], [1])` is `[[1]]`. Use `list.concat` to join two lists. `list.append` works the same way and takes several items too.
- **`min(values...)` and `max(values...)`** take one list, or two or more values, all numbers or all strings. An empty list or null gives null, so `max(xs) ?? 0` works.
- **`math.sum(list)`** adds up a list of numbers. An empty list or null gives `0`.

See the [core helpers](https://resterm.app/docs/rts/stdlib/#core-helpers) and [math helpers](https://resterm.app/docs/rts/stdlib/#math-helpers) docs.

## Standard library names without `rts.`

`list`, `dict`, `text` and `math` work at the top level, like `json` and `time` already did. You can also declare your own `json`, `len` or any other library name.

```http
### Cart
# @name cart
# @rts test "cart total"
> {%
fn price(item) {
  return item.price
}
let json = response.json()
let prices = list.map(json.items, price)
if math.sum(prices) > 20 {
  t.error("total " + str(math.sum(prices)) + " is over 20, top price " + str(max(prices)))
}
%}
GET {{base.url}}/cart
```

1.15.0 stopped at `let json`, and the script would also have needed `rts.list.map`. `math.sum` and `max` didn't exist yet:

```text
error[script]: name already defined: "json"
--> cart.http:8:1
```

Now it runs and reports the real failure:

```text
Tests:
  [FAIL] cart total - cart.http:11: total 23.75 is over 20, top price 12 (58.792µs)
```

- An `@use` alias can be a library name too, such as `json`.
- `rts`, `stdlib` and host objects such as `env` are still reserved at the top level of an `@rts` block.
- Inside `@assert`, `text()` is still the response body. Use `rts.text` for the text helpers there.

See [name precedence](https://resterm.app/docs/rts/host-objects/#name-precedence).

## Stricter `null` handling

Previosly, searching a string for `null` searched for an empty string, which every string contains. So this assertion passed when `trace.id` was never set:

```http
# @assert vars.get("trace.id") in header("X-Trace")
```

It fails in this release:

```text
error[script]: cannot search a string for null
--> order.http:3:32
     |
   3 | # @assert vars.get("trace.id") in header("X-Trace")
     |                                ^
```

The same goes for `not in` and `contains(s, null)`. Membership in lists and dictionaries hasn't changed. If a missing value should fail the assertion instead of stopping the script, check for null first:

```rts
vars.get("trace.id") != null and vars.get("trace.id") in header("X-Trace")
```

`text.startsWith`, `text.endsWith`, `text.split`, `text.replace`, `match`, `json.has` and `json.get` reject a null value to search for. In 1.15.0 they treated it as an empty string, so `text.startsWith(s, null)` was always true and `json.get(v, null)` returned the whole value. Empty strings work as before, and so does searching in null: `text.startsWith(null, "a")` is still false.

See [membership operators](https://resterm.app/docs/rts/language/#membership-operators) and [text helpers](https://resterm.app/docs/rts/stdlib/#text-helpers).

## `+` on lists and dictionaries

In 1.15.0, `+` on two lists or two dictionaries turned both into text and joined them, so `["ops"] + ["billing"]` gave the string `["ops"]["billing"]`. Now it fails with `cannot add two lists` or `cannot add two dicts`. Use `list.concat` or `append` for lists and `dict.merge` for dictionaries. Joining text, as in `"ids: " + ids`, works as before.

## `@use` and `@setting` stay in their request

An `@use` or `@setting` at the start of a `###` block belongs to that request, even before `@name` or the request line. In 1.15.0 it applied to the whole file. Two requests that imported different modules as `v` failed with `alias already defined: v`, and a one-request `base-url` changed the URL of every request in the file. `@settings` works the same way.

To share an import or setting, put it above the first `###`. A block with `@use` or `@setting` but no request warns:

```text
@setting in a block without a request was ignored. Move it above the first ### to share it
```

## Clearer error messages

Wrong argument counts give both numbers: `len(x) expects 1 argument, got 0` instead of `len(x) expects 1 args`. Your own functions show their signature, so calling `add` with one argument gives `add(a, b) expects 2 arguments, got 1` instead of `arg count mismatch`.

Errors inside a module show its path the way the request file's path is shown, such as `rts/validators.rts:7:70`, instead of the full absolute path.

## Other fixes

- `list.sort` puts NaN first. In 1.15.0, `[3, num("NaN"), 1, 2]` came back unsorted.
- `list.sort([true])` fails, as `list.sort([true, false])` already did.

## Upgrading from 1.15.0

Most scripts keep working. If you have request files, shared modules or CI checks, watch out for these:

1. `+` on two lists or dictionaries fails. Use `list.concat`, `append` or `dict.merge`.
2. `null in s`, `null not in s` and `contains(s, null)` fail when `s` is a string. 1.15.0 treated null as an empty string, so `in` and `contains` were true and `not in` was false. Check for null first, as shown above.
3. A null value to search for fails in `text.startsWith`, `text.endsWith`, `text.split`, `text.replace`, `match`, `json.has` and `json.get`, with errors such as `cannot search for a null prefix`. In 1.15.0, `startsWith`, `endsWith`, `match` and `json.has` returned true, `split` split into single characters, `replace` put the new text around every character, and `json.get` returned the whole value. Pass `""` if you relied on that.
4. `list.sort` of one item that isn't a number or string, such as `[true]` or `[null]`, fails with `list.sort(list) expects numbers or strings`. 1.15.0 returned a copy.
5. Some error messages changed. Update CI checks that match them:
   - `len(x) expects 1 args` is `len(x) expects 1 argument, got 0`.
   - `num(x[, def]) expects 1-2 args` is `num(x[, def]) expects 1 or 2 arguments, got 0`.
   - `arg count mismatch` is `add(a, b) expects 2 arguments, got 1`, with the name and counts from the call.
   - A module error shows the module path like the request file, such as `rts/validators.rts:7:70`, instead of the absolute path.
6. The new top-level names don't break anything. If your script declares its own `list` or `text`, it keeps using it.
7. An `@use` at the start of a `###` block, or after only comments there, imports the module for that request only. Another request that used it fails with `undefined name`. Move shared imports above the first `###`.
8. An `@setting` or `@settings` at the start of a `###` block applies to that request only. That includes files written by `--from-curl`, where `-k` used to turn off TLS checks for every request in the file. Move file defaults above the first `###`.
9. Like `@name`, a leading `@use` or `@setting` starts the request, so lines after it belong to that request. `@x = 1` there is a request variable, `@mock` after it is an error, and `@workflow` after it drops the `@use` or `@setting` with a warning. Put `@mock` and `@workflow` first in their block.

## Upgrading from 1.14.1 or earlier

If you're upgrading from **1.14.1** or earlier, also read the [1.15.0 release notes](https://github.com/unkn0wn-root/resterm/releases/tag/v1.15.0). They cover changes to `{% %}` blocks, JSON paths, `@rts` options, exit codes and host objects in modules.
